name: Scottish Gin
description: More than two thirds of all British gin is distilled in Scotland, and the country long ago stopped treating it as whisky's side project. Expect heather, sea pink and bog myrtle alongside the juniper.
funFact: Scotland distils roughly 70% of the UK's gin, largely because the whisky industry left the country full of stills, expertise and spare capacity.

serve.how: Build over plenty of ice with a light tonic, two parts to one, and stir once. A heather-forward Scottish gin wants a garnish that echoes it rather than fights it, so reach for grapefruit peel or a sprig of thyme instead of the usual lime.

composition.summary: Neutral grain spirit redistilled with juniper and Scottish botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit, usually wheat

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper plus heather, bog myrtle, sea pink, milk thistle

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, one-shot or concentrate

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, though barrel-rested bottlings exist

composition.process: Foraged coastal botanicals are what separate a Scottish gin from a London Dry made anywhere else.

name: Plymouth Gin
description: Softer, earthier and rounder than London Dry, with more root and less pine. It is the only English gin tied by protection to a single city, and there is only one distillery left making it.
funFact: Plymouth Gin was the specified gin in the first written Dry Martini recipes, and the Royal Navy carried it worldwide from the Black Friars Distillery, in use since 1793.

serve.how: This is the gin to make a Martini with when you want weight rather than bite. Stir with a dry vermouth at about five to one until the mixing glass frosts, strain, and express a lemon peel over the top. Its lower juniper pitch also makes it the right call in a Gimlet.

composition.summary: Wheat spirit redistilled with seven botanicals, weighted toward roots.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral wheat spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, coriander, angelica, orris root, cardamom, lemon and orange peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single copper pot still at Black Friars, Plymouth

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: A higher proportion of root botanicals gives the earthiness that defines the style.

name: English Whisky
description: England distilled whisky for centuries, stopped entirely around 1905, and started again in 2006. The new distilleries had no house style to inherit, so they invented one: fruit-forward, lightly peated when at all, and unafraid of odd casks.
funFact: English whisky received legally protected status in 2022, more than a century after the last English distillery of the old era fell silent.

serve.how: Pour a generous measure and give it a few minutes in the glass; young whisky opens quickly. A drop or two of water is worth adding at cask strength, where it pulls the orchard fruit forward out of the alcohol.

composition.summary: Malted barley, distilled and matured in England for at least three years.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, much of it Norfolk-grown

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years, often in ex-bourbon and STR casks

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–46%, with cask-strength releases common

composition.process: Warmer English summers push maturation along faster than in Scotland, so young stock tastes older than it is.

name: Pimm's No. 1
description: A gin-based fruit cup at 25%, invented by a London oyster bar owner as a digestive and now inseparable from English summer. On its own it is treacly and odd; drowned in lemonade with a fruit salad in it, it makes sense.
funFact: James Pimm served it in a small tankard called a No. 1 Cup in the 1840s, which is why the bottle still carries a number rather than a name.

serve.how: One part Pimm's to three parts chilled lemonade over a lot of ice. Then the fruit, which is not optional: cucumber ribbon, orange slice, strawberry, and a good handful of mint bruised between your palms first.

composition.summary: Gin sweetened and infused with caramelised fruit and herbal extracts.

components.label: Base
components.detail: London gin

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bitter orange, caramel, herbs and spices to a secret recipe

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: None; the base gin is infused and sweetened

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 25% ABV, built for dilution

composition.process: The recipe has stayed with six people at a time since the 1820s, or so the company says.

name: Welsh Whisky
description: Wales went without a whisky distillery for most of the twentieth century until Penderyn opened in 2004 in the Brecon Beacons. Its unusual single-copper-still design produces a notably light, floral spirit.
funFact: Penderyn uses a Faraday still designed at Surrey University that does in one pass what most distilleries need two or three stills to achieve.

serve.how: Neat first, then a few drops of water. Penderyn's Madeira-finished bottling in particular tightens up with too much dilution, so add water in small increments and stop as soon as the raisin note blooms.

composition.summary: Malted barley wash distilled in a single bespoke still and matured in Wales.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, wash bought in from a Welsh brewery

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single Faraday copper still, one pass to around 92%

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, then finished in Madeira, sherry or port

composition.process: Distilling to a very high strength in one pass makes for a lighter spirit than a conventional double pot still gives.

name: Eau-de-Vie
description: Clear, unaged fruit brandy, and the hardest category in distilling to do well. There is nowhere to hide: no wood, no sugar, no colour, just whatever the fruit gave you and whatever you did to it.
funFact: It can take around thirty kilos of raspberries to make a single bottle of framboise, which is why good eau-de-vie costs what it does.

serve.glass: Small tulip or chilled stemmed glass
serve.how: Chill the glass rather than the bottle, since a freezing spirit shows nothing. Pour about an ounce after a meal and drink it in small sips. The aroma is the entire point, so nose it well before the first taste.

composition.summary: Whole fruit fermented and distilled to preserve aroma, then rested in glass.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Raspberry, pear Williams, mirabelle, quetsch or cherry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot still, low and slow, tight heart cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None in wood; rested in glass or earthenware to soften

composition.process: Distilled to a lower strength than most spirits so that the fruit esters carry over rather than being stripped out.

name: Marc
description: France's answer to grappa, distilled from the skins, pips and stems left in the press after the wine is made. Rustic where grappa aims for finesse, and often aged in wood until it tastes closer to an old brandy.
funFact: Marc de Champagne is used far more often in kitchens than in glasses, where it flavours truffles, sorbets and the odd wedding cake.

serve.how: Serve after dinner at room temperature in a small pour. Aged marc rewards a warmed glass; young marc does not, and heat only sharpens its edges. It also does honourable work poured into an espresso.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and distilled after the wine press.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Skins, pips and stems from winemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still, often mobile and shared between growers

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Frequently oak-aged, sometimes for decades

composition.process: Because the pomace has already given up its juice, everything left is skin and structure, which is where the grip comes from.

name: Grand Marnier
description: Cognac married with bitter Caribbean orange, which puts it a class above the neutral-spirit orange liqueurs. Heavier and rounder than triple sec, and the reason a Sidecar tastes different depending on which bottle you reach for.
funFact: Created in 1880, the name was a joke by César Ritz at a time when fashion demanded everything be called petite; Marnier called his grand instead.

serve.temp: room temp or on the rocks
serve.glass: Snifter, or a coupe in a drink
serve.how: Neat in a snifter after dinner, or over a single large cube. In cocktails it belongs in a Sidecar or a Cadillac Margarita, where its cognac base adds weight that Cointreau deliberately leaves out.

composition.summary: Cognac blended with distilled bitter orange essence and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cognac, roughly half the blend

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Citrus bigaradia, the bitter orange of the Caribbean

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Orange peel macerated and distilled, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak after blending

composition.process: Using cognac rather than neutral spirit is the whole difference, and it is why the liqueur can be drunk on its own.

name: Suze
description: Yellow gentian root, dug by hand from Alpine and Jura hillsides after several years in the ground, macerated into a pale gold aperitif that is bitter in a way almost nothing else is: floral, earthy and faintly medicinal.
funFact: Picasso painted a bottle of it into a 1912 collage, Verre et bouteille de Suze, which now hangs in a university museum in St Louis.

serve.how: Over ice with tonic or soda and a slice of orange is the French café serve. In a cocktail it is the backbone of a White Negroni, standing in for Campari with gin and Lillet.

composition.summary: Gentian root macerated and distilled, then sweetened and lightly coloured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Gentiana lutea root, aged four years in the ground before harvest

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Part macerated, part distilled, then blended

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 15–20%, low for a bitter

composition.process: Gentian takes years to mature underground and is dug with a long two-pronged fork, which is why it has never been cheap.

name: Izarra
description: The Basque country's herbal liqueur, made in green and yellow versions like Chartreuse but sweeter, with armagnac underneath and a heavy hand of local plants. Izarra means star in Basque.
funFact: The recipe was assembled in 1906 by a Basque chemist who had spent years cataloguing plants in the Pyrenees before deciding what to do with them.

serve.how: Straight and cold after a meal, or poured over crushed ice as they do in Bayonne. The yellow is the gentler of the two and the better introduction; the green is stronger and more aggressively herbal.

composition.summary: Armagnac and plant distillates blended with honey and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Armagnac

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Reportedly 32 Pyrenean plants for the yellow, 48 for the green

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Plants macerated and distilled, then blended and sweetened with honey

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak

composition.process: Honey rather than sugar syrup gives it the weight that separates it from its Alpine cousins.

name: Pineau des Charentes
description: Unfermented grape must stopped in its tracks with young cognac, so it keeps the sweetness of the fruit and gains the strength of the spirit. Legend says a Charentais grower invented it in 1589 by pouring must into a barrel he thought was empty.
funFact: It must be aged at least a year in oak before sale, and the rosé version is made the same way from red grapes.

serve.how: Serve cold as an aperitif, which is how the region drinks it, rather than after dinner. It works better than most sweet wines with foie gras or melon because the cognac keeps it from cloying.

composition.summary: Fresh grape must fortified with cognac before fermentation can start.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Unfermented must from Charentais grapes

components.label: Fortification
components.detail: Cognac eau-de-vie at least one year old

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum 12 months in oak, often far longer

composition.process: Because fermentation never begins, the sugar in the grape stays in the glass.

name: Floc de Gascogne
description: Armagnac country's version of Pineau, and arguably the better drink: grape must fortified with young armagnac, which brings more grip and less polish than cognac does. Floc means bouquet of flowers in Gascon.
funFact: The appellation was only created in 1990, though Gascon farmers had been making it for their own tables for four centuries before anyone wrote it down.

serve.how: Cold, before the meal, in a small pour. The rosé is fuller and stands up to charcuterie; the white is better with melon or a slice of foie gras on toast. Do not let it sit warm, as the sweetness takes over.

composition.summary: Gascon grape must fortified with armagnac from the same estate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Unfermented must, white or red, from the Armagnac region

components.label: Fortification
components.detail: Young armagnac, typically from the producer's own stock

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least ten months, in tank or oak

composition.process: Rules require the must and the armagnac to come from the same producer, which keeps it a farmhouse product.

name: Korenwijn
description: The maltiest grade of jenever, at least 51% malt wine and usually cask-rested, which puts it closer to a young whisky than to gin. This is what gin tasted like before anyone thought to strip the grain out of it.
funFact: Tradition demands the tulip glass be filled to the brim and the first sip taken with hands behind your back, bending to the glass rather than lifting it.

serve.how: Keep the bottle in the freezer and fill the glass until it domes. Take the first sip without touching it, then drink the rest slowly. A blond lager alongside makes it a kopstootje, the Dutch boilermaker.

composition.summary: Malt wine and juniper distillate blended and rested in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malt wine from rye, corn and malted barley, at least 51%

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, with restraint

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still for the malt wine, then redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, commonly one to three years

composition.process: The malt wine is the point; the juniper is seasoning rather than the main event.

name: Beerenburg
description: A Frisian bitter built on juniper spirit and a fistful of gentian, bay and dried herbs. Invented by an Amsterdam spice merchant, adopted wholesale by the north, and drunk cold against weather.
funFact: Hendrik Beerenburg sold the herb mixture over the counter so people could steep their own jenever at home; the bottled version came much later.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass, taken before or after food rather than with it. In Friesland it is also drunk with hot water and sugar as a cure for whatever is going around.

composition.summary: Jenever or neutral spirit steeped with a fixed herb blend.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Juniper spirit or jenever

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, bay, juniper berry, laurel and a dozen more

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated rather than redistilled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 30%

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation keeps the herbs tasting green and raw instead of polished.

name: Elixir d'Anvers
description: Antwerp's herbal liqueur, made to the same recipe since 1863 by the same family in the same building. Saffron-gold, sweet on the front, and considerably more bitter on the finish than the colour suggests.
funFact: The distillery in Antwerp has never moved and still runs a museum in the same premises where François-Xavier de Beukelaer first made it.

serve.how: Neat after dinner is standard. Belgians also pour it over vanilla ice cream, and in winter mix it with hot water as a grog. It is sweet enough that a small pour goes a long way.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit distilled with 32 plants and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 32 herbs and plants, saffron among them

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then sweetened and rested

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak before bottling

composition.process: The recipe has been held by five generations of the same family and never published.

name: Mandarine Napoléon
description: Cognac infused with Sicilian mandarin peel, softer and more perfumed than an orange liqueur. The story attaches it to Napoleon's personal chemist, which is almost certainly a marketing decision made long after the fact.
funFact: Antoine-François de Fourcroy, the chemist credited with the recipe, was a real member of Napoleon's circle, though the liqueur itself was commercialised in Brussels in 1892.

serve.glass: Snifter, or coupe in a drink
serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or over ice with soda as a long aperitif. It substitutes well for triple sec in a Margarita or Sidecar when you want the drink rounder and more floral.

composition.summary: Cognac macerated with mandarin peel and spice, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cognac

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sicilian mandarin peel, plus herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and distilled, then blended into aged cognac

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested before bottling

composition.process: Mandarin peel carries a softer, sweeter oil than bitter orange, which is why this reads as perfume rather than marmalade.

name: Korn
description: German grain spirit, unaged and legally forbidden to contain anything but grain, water and yeast. No flavouring, no sweetening, no colouring. What is left is a clean spirit that tastes faintly of bread and nothing else.
funFact: Korn must be at least 32% by law, and Doppelkorn at least 38%; the rules date to a 1789 Prussian decree and have barely changed.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a tiny glass, drunk in one go with a beer to follow. In the north it is called Herrengedeck when paired with a pilsner. Ageing it in oak makes something closer to a light whisky, but that is no longer Korn.

composition.summary: Rye, wheat, barley or oats distilled to a modest strength with nothing added.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rye, wheat, barley or oats, or a blend

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, but not to full neutrality

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None permitted for the Korn designation

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 32% minimum, 38% for Doppelkorn

composition.process: Distilling below neutrality is deliberate: the grain character is the product, so stripping it out would defeat the purpose.

name: Obstler
description: The catch-all orchard brandy of southern Germany and Austria, usually apple and pear together, though the name covers whatever the trees produced. Farm-made versions are rough and honest; the good ones are as precise as any eau-de-vie.
funFact: Germany has tens of thousands of registered small distillers, most of them farms with the right to distil a fixed annual quota from their own fruit.

serve.how: Cool rather than frozen, after a heavy meal, in a small pour. Southern Germans will tell you it settles the stomach after schnitzel, and there is enough of a digestive tradition behind that to take it seriously.

composition.summary: Orchard fruit mashed, fermented and pot-distilled without added sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Apples and pears, sometimes plums or mixed orchard fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot still, usually on the farm

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Normally unaged; some rest in ash or glass

composition.process: Fruit is fermented whole on its own sugars, so a poor harvest shows up directly in the bottle.

name: Steinhäger
description: A Westphalian juniper spirit protected to the town of Steinhagen, and distinct from gin in one important way: the juniper is fermented and distilled itself rather than steeped in finished spirit. Drier, sharper and far less perfumed.
funFact: It is traditionally sold in a grey-brown stoneware crock, which is why the older bottles look more like cough medicine than a spirit.

serve.how: Freezer cold and neat, chased with a pilsner. It is a drink for cutting through fat rather than for sipping, and Westphalians serve it alongside ham rather than after it.

composition.summary: Fermented juniper berry distillate blended with grain spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain spirit plus a separate juniper berry distillate

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper alone, fermented rather than macerated

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Berries fermented and distilled, then blended and redistilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Fermenting the berries produces a rawer, greener juniper note than any maceration can.

name: Jägermeister
description: Fifty-six herbs, roots, fruits and spices macerated, filtered and rested in oak for a year before sweetening. It has spent decades being drunk cold and fast by people who have no idea it is a serious German digestive, which it is.
funFact: The name means master of the hunt, a formal German forestry title, and the stag on the label refers to the legend of Saint Hubertus.

serve.glass: Small shot glass or chilled tumbler
serve.how: The company insists on freezer temperature, and they are right: cold mutes the sweetness and lets the anise and bitter root through. Sip it rather than shoot it and it behaves like the amaro it actually is.

composition.summary: 56 botanicals macerated in alcohol and water, filtered, then oak-rested.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit and water

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 56 herbs, roots, fruits and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated over weeks, not distilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: One year in oak vats before sugar and caramel are added

composition.process: Maceration in five separate batches, then a year in wood, is what turns a bitter herbal extract into something drinkable.

name: Weinbrand
description: German brandy, softer and sweeter than cognac and generally aged in smaller casks. Hugo Asbach coined the word Weinbrand in 1907 to replace cognac on German labels after the French objected, and it stuck.
funFact: Asbach also invented the brandy bean, a chocolate filled with liquid Weinbrand, which remains a fixture of German Christmas markets.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature after dinner, or in coffee with cream. German bars also serve it long with cola, which is less of a crime than it sounds given how sweet the base spirit already is.

composition.summary: Wine distillate, mostly imported, aged in Limousin oak in Germany.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine, largely from France and Italy

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum six months, quality grades far longer, in small Limousin casks

composition.process: Smaller casks mean faster wood contact, which is where the vanilla and caramel come from.

name: Danziger Goldwasser
description: A herbal liqueur suspended with flakes of genuine 22-carat gold, first made in Danzig in 1598. The gold does nothing at all to the flavour, which was rather the point when alchemists were selling it as medicine.
funFact: Gold was thought to be medicinal in the sixteenth century, so drinking flakes of it was a health measure rather than a flourish.

serve.how: Roll the bottle gently before pouring to lift the gold back into suspension, then serve cold and neat. It is worth pouring in decent light, since watching the flakes settle is most of the experience.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit distilled with spices and herbs, sweetened, with gold leaf added.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Anise, cinnamon, cardamom, citrus peel and around twenty others

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, sweetened, then gold flakes suspended

composition.process: Gold is chemically inert, so it passes through untouched and contributes nothing but the look.

name: Eierlikör
description: German egg liqueur, thicker and richer than Dutch advocaat, and served often enough with a small spoon that the spoon is sold with it. Christmas markets run on the stuff.
funFact: It is sold at Christmas markets in edible waffle cups, which solves the problem of what to do with the glass once you have drunk it.

serve.glass: Small cup, or poured over ice cream
serve.how: Cold and thick, eaten as much as drunk. Poured over vanilla ice cream it makes a passable dessert, and whisked into cream it becomes the filling for a great many German cakes.

composition.summary: Egg yolk, sugar and brandy emulsified into a thick liqueur.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Brandy or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Egg yolk, sugar, vanilla, sometimes cream

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: None; the base spirit is emulsified with yolk

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 20%, minimum 14% by EU rule

composition.process: EU law sets a minimum egg yolk content, which is what separates it legally from a cream liqueur.

name: Underberg
description: A digestive bitter sold only in single-serve 20ml bottles wrapped in straw paper, made from herbs of 43 countries and rested in Slovenian oak. There is no large bottle, and there never has been.
funFact: The straw paper wrapper was introduced in 1949 to protect the bottle from light, and the company has kept it despite it having no modern purpose.

serve.glass: Its own bottle, or a small glass
serve.how: One bottle, after a large meal, in a single go. Germans drink it straight from the bottle without ceremony. It is emphatically not a sipping amaro; the whole design is a measured dose.

composition.summary: Herbs from 43 countries macerated in neutral spirit and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Herbs and roots sourced from 43 countries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, not distilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Several months in Slovenian oak

composition.process: Bottling at a fixed 20ml is a deliberate constraint: the product is a dose, not a measure.

name: Marillenbrand
description: Wachau apricot brandy, and the finest fruit distillate Austria makes. The Klosterneuburger apricots grown along that stretch of the Danube are small, intensely perfumed, and worth the premium the bottles command.
funFact: Wachau apricots have protected designation status, and the trees flower so early that a single bad frost can wipe out a year's production.

serve.how: Cool but not cold, in a glass with a narrow rim to hold the aroma. Nose it for a good while before drinking; a fine Marillenbrand smells more of ripe apricot than the fruit itself does.

composition.summary: Whole Wachau apricots fermented and pot-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Klosterneuburger apricots from the Wachau valley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, narrow heart cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass or steel, never wood

composition.process: Some producers ferment a portion of the stones with the fruit, which adds the marzipan note.

name: Stroh
description: An Austrian rum-based spirit, spiced and bottled as high as 80%, which is less a drink than an ingredient. It sits in every Austrian baking cupboard and most mountain huts, and it will strip paint if you are careless.
funFact: Austria had no colonies and therefore no cane, so Stroh was built in 1832 from imported spirit and flavouring to imitate the rum Austrians could not get.

serve.how: Almost nobody drinks the 80% neat, and nobody should. It belongs in Jagertee with black tea, in punch, or over apple strudel. The 38% and 40% versions are drinkable straight, cold, in very small amounts.

composition.summary: Neutral or cane spirit flavoured with vanilla and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rum and neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Vanilla, spice and caramel to a secret formula

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended rather than redistilled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 38%, 40%, 60% and 80% expressions

composition.process: Because it was designed to imitate rum rather than be one, it leans harder on spice than any cane spirit would.

name: Zirbenschnaps
description: Swiss stone pine cones, picked young and steeped in spirit until the liquid turns rose-pink and smells like a forest floor. An Alpine hut speciality that tastes far better at altitude than it does at home.
funFact: The pine cones are harvested by hand from trees growing above 1,500 metres, and a single tree may only yield enough for a few bottles.

serve.how: After a long walk, at room temperature, in a small glass. Cold flattens the resin note that is the entire reason to drink it. Austrians pour it into hut coffee when the weather turns.

composition.summary: Young stone pine cones macerated in spirit and lightly sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or clear fruit brandy

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green cones of Pinus cembra, the Swiss stone pine

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for weeks; colour and flavour extract together

composition.process: The pink colour leaches out of the cone resin and deepens the longer the maceration runs.

name: Enzian
description: Gentian root brandy, distilled rather than merely infused, which makes it drier and stranger than Suze or any of the bitter aperitifs. Earthy in a way that divides a room instantly.
funFact: Yellow gentian takes up to ten years to build a root worth digging, and wild harvesting is regulated across most of the Alps.

serve.how: Cool, neat, in a very small pour after a heavy meal. It is not a beginner's spirit and does not reward gulping. Give it time in the glass, since the earthiness settles into something closer to celery and honey.

composition.summary: Fermented gentian root distilled to a clear, dry spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Gentiana lutea or punctata root, fermented

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still; the root itself is the fermentable

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Unlike gentian liqueurs, the root is fermented and distilled rather than steeped, so there is no sugar to hide behind.

name: Damassine
description: A damson brandy from the Jura, made only from the Damassinier plum, a small dark variety that grows in the Ajoie and barely anywhere else. It carries its own protected appellation, which is rare for a spirit this obscure.
funFact: Damassine received Swiss AOP protection in 2010 after a long dispute with France, which grows the same plum on the other side of the border.

serve.how: Cool and neat in a small pour after dinner. The plum note is delicate enough that anything colder than cellar temperature will bury it. Swiss producers suggest warming the glass in your hand for a minute first.

composition.summary: Damassinier plums fermented whole and pot-distilled.

name: Appenzeller Alpenbitter
description: Forty-two alpine herbs in a recipe held by one Appenzell family since 1902 and never written down for anyone outside it. Sweeter and more approachable than most bitters, which is how it became a Swiss household fixture.
funFact: Emil Ebneter's recipe is known to a handful of family members at a time, and the company has resisted every offer to buy it out for over a century.

serve.how: Neat after a meal, or over ice with tonic in summer. In the mountains it also goes into coffee. The sweetness makes it an easier entry point than Fernet or Underberg for anyone new to bitters.
